lead: A bot is a computer that someone else controls over the network. A botnet is a group of such computers, run by one botmaster through a command-and-control channel. Botnets exist because one infected laptop is weak, but twenty thousand are a business: they can drown a website, send spam, try stolen passwords or mine crypto. Remote access attacks are how the attacker gets that first control and keeps it. You meet botnets in DDoS-for-hire pages, in credential-stuffing runs against banks and UPI apps, and in cheap CCTV cameras that join a flood without their owner knowing.
prereq: You need: 1.4 for DDoS and port scanning, and 1.5 for how the infection arrives.

sections.h3: Bot, botnet, botmaster and the C2 channel

blocks.text: A bot is a host running a small agent that an attacker controls over the network. The owner may keep using it and may never notice. A botnet is the set of all bots under one controller. The controller is the botmaster, also called the herder. The botmaster does not log in to each machine by hand. Each bot contacts a command-and-control (C2) server for orders. The C2 channel is what makes a botnet: malware with no way to receive orders is not a botnet.

items: Centralised C2: one server or a small set, often over IRC or HTTP/HTTPS. Simple to run, easy to block if found.
Peer-to-peer C2: bots talk to other bots. No single server to seize, harder to take down.
Fast flux: the C2 domain resolves to many changing IP addresses, so one blocklist entry does not stop it.
Domain generation algorithm (DGA): the bot computes many candidate domain names per day; the botmaster registers only the one that will be used.

blocks.text: A bot does not hold a connection open all day. It beacons: it sends a short check-in after every beacon interval, for example every 60 s. Jitter is a random extra delay, say 20%, added to that interval. Jitter stops the check-ins from looking like a metronome in network traffic.

blocks.where: B is the number of beacons per bot per hour; T is the beacon interval in seconds.

blocks.text: A botnet is built and used in four stages. The stages overlap; a large botnet is always recruiting.

items: Spread: the attacker infects hosts through phishing, an exploit, or a weak remote access service. Chapter 1.5 covers the malware side.
Rally: each new bot beacons to the C2 server and registers. The botmaster now has an inventory of usable machines.
Command: the botmaster sends a task to all bots or to a selected group. The task may run for minutes or months.
Monetise: the botnet is rented or used directly. Common products are DDoS-for-hire, spam, credential stuffing, click fraud and crypto mining.

blocks.text: A single bot can be sold many times. One machine may send spam at noon, join a DDoS flood at night and mine coins in between. That is why the number of bots matters less than the number of tasks the botmaster can run.

sections.h3: Remote access attacks: getting in and staying in

blocks.text: Remote access attacks target the service that is meant to let an administrator in. The attacker wants one of two things: a login that works, or a way to run commands without a login.

head: Attack
What it exploits
What the attacker gets
rows: Weak or reused passwords on port 3389
Weak passwords or stolen keys on port 22
Admin panel or database port reachable from the internet
Camera, router or DVR still on admin/admin
Uploaded script on a web server
User runs a file that opens a back channel
Entry to the whole internal network

blocks.text: The common thread is reachability. A management port open to the internet is scanned within hours. Default credentials and no MFA turn one leak into a bot. SSH, TLS and VPN protocol details are in Unit 5. Detection, including IDS and netflow monitoring, is in Unit 6.

examples.question: A credential-stuffing botnet has 20,000 bots. Each bot tries 50 logins per hour. The success rate is 0.1%. (a) How many login attempts per hour? (b) How many successful logins per hour? (c) If each bot beacons every 60 s, how many beacons per hour reach the C2 server? (d) What does blocking the C2 domain change?
steps: Bot count N = 20,000. Login attempts per bot = 50 per hour.
(a) Total attempts per hour = N × 50 = 20,000 × 50 = 10,00,000 attempts per hour.
Success rate p = 0.1% = 0.001. Successful logins per hour = 0.001 × 10,00,000 = 1000 successful logins per hour.
Beacon interval T = 60 s. Checks per bot per hour = 3600 ÷ 60 = 60.
(c) Total beacons per hour = 20,000 × 60 = 12,00,000 beacons per hour.
(d) Blocking the C2 domain stops new commands. It does not remove the bot agent. Rate limiting at the login page plus MFA reduces successful logins to 0.
examples.answer: The botnet makes 10,00,000 attempts per hour, 1000 successful logins per hour and 12,00,000 beacons per hour; blocking the C2 domain stops new commands but does not clean the bots, so rate limiting plus MFA is needed to take successes to 0.
examples.check:
N = 20000
rate = 50
p = 0.001
T = 60
attempts = N * rate
successes = p * attempts
beacons = N * (3600 // T)
print(attempts)
print(successes)
print(beacons)

traps: Bot vs virus: a virus is code that copies itself into files; a bot is a host already under remote control.
Botnet without C2: examiners expect you to name the channel. Malware that never receives orders is not a botnet.
Botnet equals DDoS: DDoS is one product. Spam, credential stuffing, click fraud and mining are also botnet work.
Blocking C2 cleans the host: it does not. The agent stays and may switch to a new domain or server.
RAT vs remote admin tool: both give remote control; the difference is consent and purpose, not the protocol.

quiz.a: A bot is a host controlled remotely by an attacker's agent. A botnet is the set of bots controlled by one botmaster through a C2 channel.
The channel a bot uses to receive orders from the botmaster, such as IRC, HTTP/HTTPS or peer-to-peer links.

quiz.q: Why does a botnet add jitter to its beacon interval?
quiz.a: Fixed-period beacons are easy to spot as a repeating pattern. Jitter adds a random delay so check-ins blend into normal traffic.
Centralised C2 has one or a few servers; it is simple but a single point of failure. Peer-to-peer C2 has bots talk to each other; it is harder to seize but harder to coordinate.

quiz.q: A botnet has 5,000 bots, each trying 40 logins per hour, with 0.2% success. Find attempts per hour and successful logins per hour.
quiz.a: Attempts = 5,000 × 40 = 2,00,000 per hour. Successes = 0.002 × 2,00,000 = 400 per hour.

quiz.q: 4,000 bots beacon every 90 s. How many beacons per hour reach the C2 server?
quiz.a: Checks per bot per hour = 3600 ÷ 90 = 40. Total = 4,000 × 40 = 1,60,000 beacons per hour.

quiz.q: A takedown seizes the C2 server and blocks its domain. Why is the botnet not gone?
quiz.a: The bots are still infected. They may use a DGA or fast flux to find a new C2, and the agent remains until each host is cleaned.

quiz.q: Why is an RDP port open to the internet a botnet recruitment risk?
quiz.a: Attackers scan for port 3389 and try weak or reused passwords. One success gives a desktop that can join a botnet without any malware file being opened.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real incident response uses DNS sinkholes: map known C2 domains to a safe server and count which internal hosts still ask for them. Threat-intelligence feeds share botnet indicators, and law-enforcement takedowns seize C2 domains or arrest operators. IoT botnets such as Mirai showed that default passwords on cameras and routers can build a flood army in hours. Search for 'botnet takedown', 'DGA detection' and 'RDP exposure' if you want the operations side.
